title: Yishtabach
hook: the closing blessing of the verses of song

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shirat HaYam, the Song of the Sea, sung every morning. Your line was the sea song every day. What far shore did you remember? Today, the last word of the verses of song, and the end of this week. Day five hundred sixty.

Every good piece of music knows how to end. The last chord of a symphony. The final chorus that everyone sings. Even a playlist has a last song you pick on purpose. Endings tell you what the whole thing was about. The verses of song have been building for a while now: the blessing for the one who spoke, David's thanks, the alphabet psalm, five hallelujahs, the sea. Then they close with a single paragraph. It doesn't add a new idea. It gathers up every word for praise it can find and stacks them, like a final chord.
screen: `ENDINGS SAY WHAT IT WAS ABOUT.` → `THE SONGS HAVE BEEN BUILDING.` → `A FINAL CHORD.`

segments.voice: It's called Yishtabach, from its first word: yishtabach shimcha la'ad malkeinu, may your name be praised forever, our king. Then the stack. To you belong song and praise, hallel and hymn, strength and dominion, victory, greatness and might, praise and glory, holiness and sovereignty, blessings and thanksgivings. Count them and you get fifteen. Commentators have connected that number to the fifteen Songs of Ascents in the Psalms, and to the fifteen steps in the Temple where, the Mishnah says, the Levites stood and sang. Notice something about the form. Most blessings start with baruch, blessed. Yishtabach doesn't. That's because it isn't a separate blessing. It's the closing half of Baruch She'amar, the blessing that opened the verses of song. The two are bookends around everything in between, and the custom is not to talk between them. Look at the opening words in Hebrew, too. The first letters of shimcha, la'ad, malkeinu and ha'el spell Shlomo, Solomon, and a tradition credits him with the prayer. That may be a later reading, but it shows how closely people have looked at every word. And the very last phrase is lovely. It calls God habocher b'shirei zimrah: the one who chooses songs of praise. Not the one who demands them. The one who chooses them. As if, out of everything in the world, the songs people sing are something God picks out and wants.
screen: `MAY YOUR NAME BE PRAISED FOREVER.` · `FIFTEEN WORDS OF PRAISE.` · `BOOKENDS WITH BARUCH SHE'AMAR.` · `THE ONE WHO CHOOSES SONGS.` · then, large: `PRAISED FOREVER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: end one task with praise. Settle, and breathe. Think of the last thing you finished today: a meal, a shift, a phone call, this lesson. Before moving on, give it an ending. Name one good thing in it. Then another. Stack them, the way Yishtabach stacks its words: it was warm, it was useful, someone laughed, it's done. If you pray, you can close with the words yishtabach shimcha la'ad, may your name be praised forever. The bell holds the time.
Yishtabach. May it be praised: the blessing that closes the verses of song with fifteen words of praise.

Your line: praised forever. A week of the verses of song: the one who spoke, give thanks, gladness, nun, five hallelujahs, the sea, and Yishtabach. Today, end your workday with three good things, stacked. Day five hundred sixty.

howItsDone: Yishtabach closes the verses of song every morning, often said standing; it is followed by half Kaddish and the call to prayer, Barchu, which opens the Shema and its blessings.

what a scholar hears: Yishtabach is the closing blessing paired with Baruch She'amar (hence no opening baruch); its fifteen terms are tied to Psalms 120–134 and the fifteen steps of Mishnah Middot 2:5.

notes: Fifteen terms of praise counted from the standard text (shir, shevachah, hallel, zimrah, oz, memshalah, netzach, gedulah, gevurah, tehilah, tiferet, kedushah, malchut, berachot, hoda'ot); confirm.
Links of fifteen to the Songs of Ascents and the fifteen Temple steps (Mishnah Middot 2:5; Sukkah 5:4, Levites singing on them): commentary tradition (e.g. Abudarham); confirm.
Initials שלמה (shimcha la'ad malkeinu ha'el) and the attribution to Solomon: a traditional reading; presented as 'a tradition'. Confirm.
Yishtabach as closing blessing of Baruch She'amar and the custom not to interrupt between them; confirm.
